paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Barrett took place in Elkhart, Indiana, on October 27, 1888, when a crowd tried to seize a police officer who had just shot and killed a fellow officer, William Burton. The sheriff held Barrett in a saloon while the mayor and sheriff spoke to the crowd, a rainstorm scattered it, and Barrett was driven to the county jail at Goshen. The killing of one officer by another and the near-lynching that followed ran as a wire story in papers from Minnesota to California and the Dakotas.

According to a special dispatch to the Indianapolis Journal, Mayor Goldthwait had recently reprimanded Barrett, an "old officer," for continued intoxication. On the night of October 26 Barrett waylaid the mayor and whipped him severely, and he was placed under $1,000 bond to appear at the Circuit Court. The Inter-Ocean's dispatch, as printed in the St. Paul Daily Globe, said the reprimand had come only the day before and that Barrett was bound over on the morning of the shooting.

On the afternoon of October 27, having found no bondsman and being "partially intoxicated," Barrett drew a revolver on Officer Sutton, who tried to arrest him. A few minutes later Marshal Needham and Officer Burton tried to arrest him, and when Burton grasped him from behind, Barrett fired five shots. One struck Burton behind the left eye and killed him instantly, while others took off the end of Councilman Stears's finger, grazed Needham's head and passed through a man's hat. Needham and Councilman Wagner fired back, though it was not known whether Barrett was hit.

Sheriff Chatten then overpowered Barrett, forced him into a saloon and fastened the door, while "the enraged mob procured a rope and endeavored to get at the murderer to lynch him." The mayor and the sheriff addressed the crowd and quieted it somewhat, and a heavy rainstorm then broke up the gathering. Before the crowd could re-form, Barrett was put in a carriage and driven to the county jail at Goshen, where he arrived safely. The Inter-Ocean version said Barrett "took refuge" in the saloon and credited the "prompt interference of the mayor and other policemen" with saving his life.
No report of arrests among the crowd, or of an indictment or trial of Barrett, appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal ran its own special under the headline "Deadly Work with the Pistol," calling Barrett "the murderer" and the "infuriated man" and writing that the rain "fortunately" dispersed the mob. It closed by noting that Burton left a wife and young family and that Barrett also had a family and "has been considered a good officer." The Inter-Ocean dispatch appeared the next day in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "Bloodthirsty Barrett" and in the Los Angeles Daily Herald as "An Ex-Policeman's Revenge."

A shortened version headed "A Murderous Officer" ran in weekly papers in Dakota Territory and Wyoming as late as November 10. The Connecticut Western News reduced the story to a single sentence in a news-in-brief column, saying the killer had been "just dismissed from the force" and that the people were roused "to the point of attacking the jail." None of the reports named the race of anyone involved.

The Connecticut brief placed the mob at the jail and described Barrett as already dismissed, while the Indianapolis special and the wire both called him a serving officer and placed the crowd outside a saloon, from which he was taken safely to jail. The two fuller reports were datelined Elkhart on the day of the shooting and are the stronger evidence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Barrett
bases: A crowd procured a rope and tried to reach a man held by the sheriff in order to lynch him, but was quieted and dispersed and no one was killed by the mob (A1, A2).

A mob acting on Barrett's killing of Officer Burton tried to lynch him, but the mayor, sheriff and a rainstorm stopped it and he reached the Goshen jail alive (A1, A2); an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
The Indianapolis Journal's own special (A1) and the separate Inter-Ocean wire dispatch (A2) agree on the shooting, the crowd moving to lynch Barrett at a saloon, and his removal to Goshen.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal, under 'Deadly Work with the Pistol,' called Barrett 'the murderer' and the mob 'enraged,' said the rain 'fortunately' dispersed it, and noted both men's families.
The Inter-Ocean dispatch ran as 'Bloodthirsty Barrett' (St. Paul) and 'An Ex-Policeman's Revenge' (Los Angeles), crediting officials with saving his life.
Weeklies in Dakota and Wyoming ran a condensed version headed 'A Murderous Officer'; a Connecticut weekly reduced it to one news-in-brief sentence.
